title: [ATen] Handle vectorized_loop tail with masked vop, not scalar op (#197018)
body:
Summary:
X-link: https://github.com/pytorch/executorch/pull/22882


Within vectorized_loop, also use vectorized vop for the scalars in the tensor's tail.

Otherwise, the same f(x) can give different results depending on the input's position within the tensor

Test Plan: CI

Differential Revision: D120020856

items.author: ezyang
items.body: Review automatically exported from Phabricator review in Meta.

items.author: ezyang
items.body:
Review by Astra agent.

Found two numerical regressions, detailed inline. Both were reproduced in a standalone C++ harness using this PR's headers on ARM; the full PyTorch build and test suite were not run.

items.author: ezyang
items.body:
[P2] Compute float32 arange lanes in the accumulator dtype before narrowing

`Vectorized<float>::arange` takes a float base, whereas the scalar lambda computes each element in double before narrowing. Moving short tensors onto this path makes `torch.arange(16777217, 16777215, -1, dtype=torch.float32)` return `[16777216, 16777215]` instead of `[16777216, 16777216]`: the starting value is rounded before the lane offset is added. The new reduced-precision handling does not cover float32's double accumulator. Please compute the lanes in the accumulator dtype and narrow afterward, and add a regression test.

— Astra agent

items.author: ezyang
items.body:
[P2] Exclude Half from the clang fused multiply-add branch

On ARM with native FP16, `vec::fmadd<Half>` uses `vfmaq_f16`, eliminating the intermediate rounding that scalar `Half` multiplication requires. For `torch.addr(self, vec1, vec2, beta=1.0009765625, alpha=1)` with `self=[[1.0009765625]]`, `vec1=[-1.001953125]`, and `vec2=[1]` (all tensors float16), the scalar result is `0`, but this fused vector expression produces `9.53674316e-07`. This contradicts the stated intent to preserve the scalar lambda's rounding and now affects short tensors as well. Please use the unfused expression for `Half` and add a regression test on native-FP16 ARM.

— Astra agent
items.diff_hunk:
@@ -8,8 +8,37 @@
 #include <ATen/native/cpu/Loops.h>
 #include <c10/util/irange.h>
 
+// gcc defaults to -ffp-contract=fast, which fuses the multiply-add in
+// `addr_kernel` even across the rounding `c10::Half`'s operators impose. That
+// drops a rounding step the reference implementations keep, leaving float16 an
+// ulp off on hardware with native fp16. No source-level barrier blocks the
+// fusion -- `beta * self + x` is itself a fusable pair -- so this has to be
+// file-scoped, and float and double give up their fma as a result. clang and
+// MSVC (/fp:strict, see cmake/Codegen.cmake) honour the rounding already.
+#if defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(__clang__)
+#pragma GCC optimize("fp-contract=off")
+#endif
+
 namespace at::native { namespace {
 
+// Must mirror whatever the compiler did to the scalar lambda in `addr_kernel`:
+// clang contracts the float and double cases but leaves c10::Half alone, MSVC
+// contracts nothing under /fp:strict, and gcc contracts nothing thanks to the
+// pragma above. This has to be a function rather than an `#if` in the lambda
+// itself: the lambda is an AT_DISPATCH macro argument, and a preprocessor
+// directive inside a macro argument is undefined -- MSVC rejects it outright.
+template <typename T>
+inline Vectorized<T> mul_add(
+    const Vectorized<T>& a,
+    const Vectorized<T>& b,
+    const Vectorized<T>& acc) {
+#if defined(_MSC_VER) || (defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(__clang__))
+  return a * b + acc;
+#else
+  return vec::fm [truncated]

items.author: ezyang
items.body:
Could we split the numerical fixes at the call sites into separate preparatory changes, with focused regression tests, and then switch the vectorized-loop tail to `vop`?

The tail switch exposes existing differences between scalar and vector implementations even for small tensors: exponent narrowing in `pow`, intermediate rounding in `arange`, signed-zero handling in `clamp`, and FMA contraction in `addr`/`addcmul`. Fixing those first would make the intended numerical behavior explicit and let reviewers assess each fix independently of the loop change. In particular, the compiler-specific FMA handling deserves its own review and tests, since it attempts to match compiler-dependent scalar rounding.

— Astra agent

items.author: Nicoshev
items.body: Yes, some FMA operations may be wrong by 1 bit. Problem is that doing double FMA on vectorized code requires upcasting, doing FMA, downcasting. It makes the vectorized code much slower, just to avoid a precision that is currently live in prod

items.author: Nicoshev
ezyang
items.body:
@Nicoshev The concern here is premature rounding of the starting value, rather than a one-bit difference from FMA. Cancellation can amplify it into a large error in the final result. For example:

```python
torch.arange(16777217, -16777215, -16777216, dtype=torch.float32)
# Existing scalar path: [16777216, 1]
# PR's ARM vector path: [16777216, 0]
```

The scalar calculation produces the second element as `float32(16777217 - 16777216) == 1`. The vector path first rounds its base to `16777216`, then subtracts `16777216`, producing `0`. Even a correctly rounded float32 FMA cannot recover the lost starting-value bit. This is not a one-ULP error in the output, and downstream reciprocals or zero tests can behave qualitatively differently.

I reproduced these calculations in a standalone ARM intrinsic harness using the same vector arithmetic as the PR; I have not run this example in a full build of the PR. The existing vector path already exposes longer inputs to this problem, but the tail switch extends it to this previously scalar two-element input.

Could we add this as a regression test and preserve the accumulator-precision result for this case? I understand the performance concern with widening every vector, but it needs to be weighed against this cancellation behavior, not just a one-bit output discrepancy. This can be addressed within the combined PR.

— Astra agent

items.author: ezyang
items.body:
```
• The divergence happens when the vector base is passed into arange, before any
  lane offset is added. FMA does not affect this particular example.

  For CPU float32, accscalar_t is double. So initially:

  start = 16777217.0;  // exact double
  step = -1.0;        // exact double
  idx = 0;

  The scalar lambda computes each complete element in double, then converts to
  float:

   Element    Double calculation                Float32 result
  ━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
   0          16777217 + (-1) * 0 = 16777217    16777216
  ─────────  ────────────────────────────────  ────────────────
   1          16777217 + (-1) * 1 = 16777216    16777216

  Why does the first value round down? Above 2^24 = 16777216, float32 spacing is
  2. 16777217 is halfway between 16777216 and 16777218; ties-to-even selects
  16777216.

  The vector path instead calls:

  Vectorized<float>::arange(start + step * idx, step);

  Its signature (aten/src/ATen/cpu/vec/vec256/vec256_float.h:79) is:

  template <typename step_t>
  static Vectorized<float> arange(float base, step_t step);

  base is float even though step_t is deduced as double. Argument conversion
  therefore gives:

  base = 16777216.0f;  // Already lost the +1!
  step = -1.0;        // Still double

  The vector constructor computes lanes as base, base + step, etc.:

   Lane    Calculation inside arange             Float32 result
  ━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
   0       Already-rounded base                  16777216
  ──────  ────────────────────────────────────  ────────────────
   1       double(base) + step = 16777216 - 1    16777215

  16777215 is exactly representable: it is below 2^24, where float32 spacing is
  still 1. Promoting the rounded base back to double cannot recover the lost +1.

  Thus:

  Scalar: round_float(start + step * lane)
  Vector: round_float(double(round_float(start)) + step * lane)

  The comment’s “stepping … accumulates error across the lanes” can obscure
  this: these implementations calculate lane offsets independently, rather than
  repeatedly adding the step. This example is premature rounding of the base.

  Your pasted change is not in the current checkout, so this traces what happens
  if the two-element tensor enters that vector path; it does not verify that
  routing change itself.

```

items.author: ezyang
items.body: Everything here is good except the FMA treatment. In FMA we should either consistently FMA or not across all CPU archs. Because addr FMA is ambiguous, I think it would be better to match it x86 (which might not do FMA?) But I also don't hate matching CUDA's FMA behavior too. But in any case, consistency, and explicit control, are the requests.
